newsitem.title: USA: U.S., foreign banks face year 2000 challenge.
newsitem.headline: U.S., foreign banks face year 2000 challenge.

text.p: U.S. and foreign banks are racing to upgrade financial transactions systems by the year 2000 and failure to meet that deadline may result in turn-of-the millennium doom, experts said on Monday.

"The main problem in the financial services industry is that there is not a transaction that does not have a date associated with it," said Jeffrey Barnes, a director at IMI Systems, a consulting firm specialized in the 2000 issue.
Barnes spoke to Reuters at a conference of the Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade.
"The date associated with financial transactions is a critical element in the risk associated with that transaction," Barnes noted.

Many programs used by financial institutions -- mainly those five or more years old -- read only the last two digits in any given year, an important feature that determines, for instance, when interest rates are paid or due.

Experts have acknowledged the double-zero reading for the year 2000 will confuse scores of computer programs unable to figure out whether the transaction is to be conducted in January 1900 or in January 2000.
The Federal Reserve, one of the banks' supervisor, has issued compliance instructions for the banking industry to correct the problem by 1998.

"There are an estimated three billion lines of codes or computer instructions in the U.S. banking industry that are transaction-oriented, meaning they have a date attached to them," said Barnes who estimated that only about one billion instructions are ready for the new millennium.
Adding to the problem is the fact that many old computer programs are written in COBOL, a computer language so outdated that many young programmers are not used to working with it anymore.
"The banking industry is bringing programmers out of retirement or importing them from foreign countries to work on these programs," Barnes added.

The "millennium bug" has proven a windfall for programmers from less high-tech oriented nations -- such as the former Soviet republics, said Barnes who predicted "these programmers who have seen their salaries jump from $350 to $700 a day will command $1000 a day as the deadline nears."
Failure to meet the 2000 deadline may have very serious consequences for financial services participants who could find themselves cut out from the industry.

Financial services providers who will update their systems in time are likely not to deal with other institutions -- in the United States or abroad -- that have not updated their systems because of the risk of data pollution.

"It's the same problem for every bank. It's not a political deadline like the single European currency, it's a time event, a test of who will be ready," said Consider Ross, senior vice president at The Northern Trust Co.
"It's a very important consideration for our clients," added Ross, referring to the need to avoid systemic risk through transmission of faulty instructions.

Juergen Thode, senior manager at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt, said the turn of the millennium combined with the single European currency will bring a dual challenge to the industry and force some players out of the global field.

"This will be a consolidation process. Acquisitions (in the banking industry) will be going forward," said Thode who also expected banks to choose the most technology-savy counterparts as correspondent banks across continents and market segments.
Thode also predicted banks that would meet the challenges of the 1999 European Monetary Union and the millennium will become providers of services for their less sophisticated competitors.
"This will provide opportunities to offer new services to those who need to outsource products to meet their clientele's needs," Thode added.
